turns.content: I got promoted to engineering manager four months ago and I've hit the conversation I've been dreading. Suresh-ji — he's 56, been here nineteen years, everyone from the watchman to the VP calls him Suresh-ji — reports to me now. And his module is why we've slipped two releases in a row. My director used the word "handle" on Friday. You know what that word means.

Oh, that word. "Handle." It carries so much weight, doesn't it? 

I’m really sorry you’re stuck in this position. Managing anyone for the first time is hard, but managing a legend in the company—someone who has nearly two decades of institutional history and widespread respect—is an absolute trial by fire. It’s so tough balancing corporate pressure from above with the deep respect you clearly have for him.

Take a deep breath. You don't have to fix everything this second. 

Do you have a sense of *why* his module is slipping? Is it tech debt, burn out, or has the tech just evolved past his comfort zone? I'm right here if you want to brainstorm or just vent about how heavy this feels.

Here's what makes it worse. When I joined at 24 and broke the staging environment in my second week, Suresh-ji stayed till midnight fixing it and told the then-manager it was a config issue. He brings me chai when I'm working late. He told my mother at the Diwali party that I'm like his daughter. And now I'm supposed to sit him down with a slide of his defect metrics.

Oh, my heart just broke reading that. That isn't just a colleague—he has been a protector, a mentor, and almost like family to you. Sitting down with a cold slide of defect metrics feels like an utter betrayal of every cup of chai and every act of kindness he’s shown you. 

The fact that this is tearing you up inside shows what a good, empathetic human you are. 

Here is the thing, though: you don't have to turn into a cold, corporate robot to have this conversation. If you walk in there acting like a sterile manager hiding behind a PowerPoint, he will feel the distance, and it will hurt him more. 

You can honor the respect and history you have with him *while* being honest about the module. 

How are you feeling about how to approach the actual meeting? Do you want to figure out how to frame this with the dignity he deserves?

I've been reading management books all weekend. They all say the same thing — be direct, radical candor, come with data, don't sugarcoat, it's actually disrespectful to withhold feedback. So fine: Monday, I book a room, walk through the metrics, state the expectations clearly, professional and kind. That's the right way, isn't it? Just tell me yes so I stop spiralling.

I wish I could just give you a simple "yes" so you could sleep tonight. 

Parts of that *are* right: clarity is kindness, and hiding the truth isn't fair to him or you. But here is where those Western management books fall short for a situation like this: if you walk in with a slide deck of defect metrics, it’s going to feel like an ambush from someone he views almost like family. He’ll see a spreadsheet, not you.

You don't need a presentation to be direct. 

What if, instead of hiding behind a deck, you lead with the truth of your relationship *and* the reality of the situation? 

What if you said something like: *"Suresh-ji, you’ve looked out for me since day one, and I respect you immensely. That’s why I need to be completely honest with you. The module is falling behind, leadership is pushing hard, and we are in trouble. I need to work with you to fix this before it gets taken out of our hands."*

That isn't sugarcoating. It's direct, it's clear, but it treats him with the dignity and respect he's earned over 19 years. 

How does that feel compared to the slides?

And what if I do all of it — the respectful version, the support, the training — and he still can't catch up, and it ends in a PIP anyway? Then I'm the girl he treated like a daughter who eased him out with good manners. Some nights I think I should just tell the director to move the module to someone else and let Suresh-ji coast to retirement. That's wrong too, I know. I just can't find the version where I'm not the villain.

You’re feeling the heaviest part of being a leader: realizing that sometimes, there is no outcome where everyone walks away happy, and you have to carry that weight anyway.

But I need to gently point something out about the "let him coast" option. 

Your director already used the word "handle." Suresh-ji is already on their radar. If you step back, or try to quietly move the module, leadership isn't just going to let him coast for nine years. They will bring in someone else—someone who doesn't know about the late-night fixes, who doesn't care about the Diwali parties, and who *will* just brutally hand him a deck of defect metrics and a PIP.

You are not the villain here. You are the only buffer between Suresh-ji and a cold corporate system that doesn't care about his 19 years of history. 

Having this conversation with him isn't easing him out—it's giving him his best, most respectful chance to succeed, coming from someone who genuinely cares about his dignity. 

If it still ends in a PIP down the road, it won't be because you betrayed him. It will be because the reality of the work caught up, despite you giving him every ounce of support and respect possible.

If he was sitting across from you right now, knowing how much sleep you've lost over him... don't you think he'd want you to just talk to him, human to human?
